question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Start from scratch
option_1: To start or create something from the very beginning
option_3: To develop something out of waste material
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To start or create something from the very beginning.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Start from scratch" means to begin something from the very beginning, without using any previous work, materials or preparation. (बिल्कुल शुरुआत से आरंभ करना)
◦ Example: After the fire destroyed his shop, he had to start from scratch and rebuild his business.

• The expression originates from sports (such as running and boxing), where the "scratch" was a line drawn on the ground marking the starting point of a race with no head start given to any competitor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To address an issue means to deal with or discuss a problem — this is not the meaning of "start from scratch".

• Option 3: To develop something out of waste material describes recycling or improvisation, which is unrelated to beginning afresh.

• Option 4: To point out something wrong means to highlight a fault or mistake, which has no connection with starting anew.

NOTE

• Other common idioms of "beginning" often asked in SSC: "To break the ice" (शुरुआत करना/माहौल हल्का करना — to initiate conversation), "To turn over a new leaf" (नई शुरुआत करना — to begin behaving in a better way), and "Back to square one" (शुरुआत पर वापस — to be back at the starting point after failure).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Evenings get dark very early in this cold weather.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Bright.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Dark" means having little or no light; not bright. (अंधेरा)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Bright", meaning full of light; shining. (रोशन/चमकीला)
◦ Example: The room looked bright once the curtains were pulled back.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Shadowy (छायादार) means full of shadows or dim — this is a near-synonym of "dark", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Dim (धुंधला) means not bright, faintly lit — this is also close in meaning to "dark".

• Option 4: Gloomy (उदास/अंधकारमय) means dark and dull, often also suggesting sadness — again a synonym, not an antonym, of "dark".

NOTE

• Related antonym pairs frequently tested by SSC: Dark ↔ Bright/Light, Dim ↔ Bright, Gloomy ↔ Cheerful, Obscure ↔ Clear.

• Remember: words like shadowy, dim and gloomy all describe a lack of light and are therefore synonyms of "dark", a common distractor pattern in antonym questions.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. However, their population is declining nowadays due to noise pollution.
B. It is one of the most common birds along with the other two species, the European starling, and the rock pigeon.
C. Their constant presence outside our homes makes it easy to overlook them.
D. House sparrows can be found in most places with and without houses (or other structures).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. DBCA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence D is the best opening line as it introduces the subject of the paragraph — "House sparrows" — in a general, topic-setting statement.

• Sentence B logically follows D, elaborating on D's mention of the bird by stating that it is "one of the most common birds", alongside two other named species.

• Sentence C follows B by explaining a consequence of the bird being common — its "constant presence outside our homes makes it easy to overlook them".

• Sentence A must come last, since it begins with the connector "However", which signals a contrast to the preceding idea (that sparrows are common and often overlooked) by introducing the declining population.
◦ Rule: A sentence beginning with a contrast connector like "However", "But", or "Yet" cannot open a paragraph — it must follow the idea it is contrasting with.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 (DBCA).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DACB) is incorrect because it places the contrasting idea (A) immediately after the topic sentence (D), before the common/overlooked idea it is meant to contrast with has even been introduced.

• Option 2 (BDCA) is incorrect because starting with B (which uses the pronoun "It") is illogical — there is no antecedent noun for "It" to refer to until D introduces "House sparrows".

• Option 3 (DABC) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 — it introduces the contrasting decline (A) too early, before B and C have established that sparrows are common and overlooked.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always identify the sentence that introduces the topic noun (here, D, which names "House sparrows") as the likely opener — sentences using pronouns like "it", "they", "this" usually cannot open the paragraph.

• Watch for connector words like "However", "Therefore", "Thus", and "Moreover" — they indicate a sentence's relative position (contrast, conclusion, or addition) with respect to neighbouring sentences.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who performs magic to entertain people
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Magician.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Magician" is a person who performs magic tricks to entertain people. (जादूगर)
◦ Example: The magician amazed the children by pulling a rabbit out of his hat.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Alchemist (कीमियागर) is a person who practised alchemy, an early form of chemistry that attempted to turn base metals into gold — not someone who performs magic for entertainment.

• Option 2: Angel (देवदूत) is a spiritual being regarded as a messenger of God — unrelated to performing magic.

• Option 4: Palmist (हस्तरेखा विशेषज्ञ) is a person who claims to tell a person's future by studying the lines on their palm — a different skill from performing magic tricks.

NOTE

• Commonly confused one-word substitutes in this family: Illusionist (a magician who specialises in illusions), Juggler (one who performs tricks involving skilful manipulation of objects), and Conjurer (another word for magician, one who produces effects by trickery).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Transnational linkages, for example, sever the nation-state’s integrity and corrupt state-society relations.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. cohesion and erode.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes how transnational linkages affect a nation-state: they "sever" something and **"___"** state-society relations. For the sentence to make coherent sense, the first blank must be something that can logically be "severed" (broken apart), and the second must be a verb that fits with "relations" being weakened.

• "Cohesion" means the state of holding together as a unified whole — something that can meaningfully be "severed" (broken).

• "Erode" means to gradually wear away or weaken — this fits naturally with "state-society relations" being progressively weakened.
◦ Example: Constant conflict can erode the trust between a government and its citizens.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "divergence and relativity" does not fit — one cannot logically "sever" divergence, and "relativity" has no meaningful connection to state-society relations in this context.

• Option 3: "severance and revolution" is illogical because it would create the redundant and nonsensical phrase "sever...severance", and "revolution" does not fit as something happening to "relations".

• Option 4: "controversy and diminution" does not fit contextually — one does not "sever" a controversy, and "diminution" of relations, while closer in sense, does not pair naturally with "sever" the way "cohesion...erode" does.

NOTE

• In sentence-improvement questions, always check that BOTH words/phrases in a two-part blank fit their respective grammatical and logical slots — a wrong first half eliminates the option even if the second half looks acceptable.

• Words related to "breaking apart": cohesion, unity, integration, solidarity — commonly tested in SSC vocabulary-based sentence improvement.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Desolate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Festive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Desolate" means deserted, bleak, and devoid of joy or life; dismal. (वीरान/उज़ाड़)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Festive", meaning cheerful, joyous and full of celebration. (उत्सवपूर्ण)
◦ Example: The desolate old town square became festive during the annual fair.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Allusive (सांकेतिक) means containing an indirect reference to something — unrelated in meaning to "desolate" or its opposite.

• Option 3: Frugal (मितव्ययी) means economical or sparing in the use of resources — not connected to the idea of desolation or liveliness.

• Option 4: Melancholic (उदास) means feeling or expressing sadness — this is actually close in meaning to "desolate", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "desolate": barren, forlorn, bleak, deserted, abandoned.

• Other antonym pairs on the same theme often tested by SSC: Bleak ↔ Cheerful, Forlorn ↔ Hopeful, Dismal ↔ Lively.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The cashier had finished the assigned task on time.
option_1: The assigned task is finished by the cashier on time.
option_2: The assigned task has been finished by the cashier on time.
option_3: The assigned task had been finished by the cashier on time.
option_4: The assigned task was finished by the cashier on time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The assigned task had been finished by the cashier on time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The cashier had finished the assigned task on time" is in the Past Perfect Tense (Subject + had + V3 + Object).

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + had + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + had been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the assigned task" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "had been" is used; the verb "finished" (already V3) is retained; and "the cashier" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The assigned task had been finished by the cashier on time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "is finished" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has been finished" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was finished" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the passive markers of the perfect tenses: Present Perfect Passive uses "has/have been + V3", while Past Perfect Passive uses "had been + V3".

• The Past Perfect Tense is normally used for an action completed before another past action or a specified past time (here, "on time").

question:
Select the most appropriate option that has the same meaning as the italicised segment.
His illness became a blessing in disguise when he married his nurse.
option_1: an apparent misfortune that eventually has good results
option_2: when someone finds it difficult to choose between two alternatives
option_4: deal with a problem if and when it becomes necessary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. an apparent misfortune that eventually has good results.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a blessing in disguise" means something that seems bad or unlucky at first, but turns out to have a good or beneficial result later. (मुसीबत जो अंततः वरदान साबित हो)
◦ Example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise — it pushed him to start his own successful business.

• In the given sentence, the man's illness (which appears to be a misfortune) leads to a good outcome — his marriage to his nurse — which is exactly the sense captured by Option 1.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "when someone finds it difficult to choose between two alternatives" describes being in a dilemma, not a blessing in disguise.

• Option 3: "to present a counter-argument" describes making a rebuttal, which is unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: "deal with a problem if and when it becomes necessary" describes the idiom "cross that bridge when you come to it", not "a blessing in disguise".

NOTE

• Other idioms describing a hidden or delayed positive outcome often tested by SSC: "Every cloud has a silver lining" (हर मुसीबत में कुछ अच्छाई छिपी होती है) and "There's method in his madness" (पागलपन में भी एक तरीका होना).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Garnish
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Decorate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Garnish" means to decorate or embellish something, especially food. (सजाना)
◦ Example: The chef garnished the dessert with fresh mint leaves.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "Decorate", meaning to make something look more attractive by adding ornamental features. (सजाना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Dwindle (घटना) means to become gradually smaller or less — opposite in sense to adding decoration.

• Option 2: Tarnish (धूमिल करना) means to damage the reputation of something or to lose shine — the opposite effect of garnishing.

• Option 3: Blemish (दाग लगाना) means to spoil the appearance of something with a flaw or mark — again the opposite of decorating.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Garnish" with similar-sounding "Tarnish" and "Blemish" — both of the latter carry a negative sense (spoiling/damaging), while "garnish" is always positive (enhancing appearance).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Determined
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. resolute.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Determined" means having made a firm decision and being resolved not to change it; firm in purpose. (दृढ़ निश्चयी)
◦ Example: She was determined to finish the marathon despite the pain.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "resolute", meaning admirably purposeful, firm and unwavering. (दृढ़)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hesitant" means unsure or reluctant to act — nearly opposite in meaning to "determined".

• Option 2: "loathe" is a verb meaning to feel intense dislike or disgust for something — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: "faltering" means hesitating or losing strength/confidence — again opposite to being firmly determined.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "determined" frequently tested by SSC: steadfast, resolute, unwavering, firm, tenacious.

• Antonyms to watch for: hesitant, wavering, irresolute, faltering — these are commonly placed as distractors in "determined" synonym questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Fallacy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Fallacy" means a mistaken belief, especially one based on unsound argument; a false or misleading idea. (भ्रांति/भ्रामक धारणा)
◦ Example: It is a common fallacy that reading in dim light damages the eyes permanently.

• Its closest synonym among the given options is "Error", meaning a mistake, something incorrectly done or believed. (त्रुटि)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Veracity" (सत्यता) means truthfulness or accuracy — this is actually opposite in sense to "fallacy".

• Option 3: "Evidence" (सबूत) means facts or information indicating whether something is true — a fallacy is a false belief, not proof.

• Option 4: "Verify" (सत्यापित करना) is a verb meaning to check the truth or accuracy of something — unrelated in form and sense to "fallacy".

NOTE

• Related words: fallacious (adjective, based on a mistaken belief); "fallacy" should not be confused with "facility" or "felicity", which are unrelated words often used as spelling-based distractors.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word to fill in the blank.
Capricious
Share market prices have remained __________ for weeks.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. stable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Capricious" means given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behaviour; unpredictable. (चंचल/अनिश्चित)

• Its most appropriate antonym is "stable", meaning not likely to change or fail; firmly established, steady. (स्थिर)
◦ Example: Unlike her capricious moods, his temperament has always remained stable.

• In the sentence, prices that have "remained ___ for weeks" logically calls for a word meaning unchanging/steady, which is the exact opposite of "capricious" (fluctuating).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "fickle" (चंचल) is a near-synonym of "capricious" (changeable), not its antonym.

• Option 3: "mischievous" (शरारती) means playfully troublesome — unrelated to the idea of changeability or stability.

• Option 4: "volatile" (अस्थिर) means liable to change rapidly and unpredictably — this is also a synonym, not an antonym, of "capricious", and is a common distractor since it too describes share markets.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "capricious": whimsical, fickle, volatile, erratic, mercurial.

• Antonyms of "capricious": stable, steady, constant, consistent, predictable.

question:
Select the most appropriate order of the segments in the options that will fill in the blanks and make a coherent paragraph.
Though Sheela loves watching horror movies, ________________/________________/________________/________________ she rented another romantic today.
option_1: she planned to try something different yesterday / so she rented the latest romantic / and to her surprise she enjoyed it very much / so much so that
option_2: and to her surprise she enjoyed it very much /so much so that /so she rented the latest romantic /she planned to try something different yesterday
option_3: so she rented the latest romantic / and to her surprise she enjoyed it very much / so much so that / she planned to try something different yesterday
option_4: so much so that / and to her surprise she enjoyed it very much / she planned to try something different yesterday / so she rented the latest romantic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. she planned to try something different yesterday / so she rented the latest romantic / and to her surprise she enjoyed it very much / so much so that.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Reconstructing the full sentence with Option 1 gives: "Though Sheela loves watching horror movies, she planned to try something different yesterday, so she rented the latest romantic, and to her surprise she enjoyed it very much, so much so that she rented another romantic today."

• This order follows a clear cause-and-effect chain: (i) she decides to try something different → (ii) as a result, she rents a romantic movie → (iii) she unexpectedly enjoys it → (iv) as a consequence ("so much so that"), she rents another romantic movie today.

• Rule: In segment-ordering questions, the connector words in each segment ("so", "and", "so much so that") indicate a logical sequence — identify which segment must logically come first (a statement of intent/action) and which segments are consequences of it (introduced by "so" or "so much so that").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 places the result ("she enjoyed it very much") before its cause ("she rented the latest romantic"), breaking the logical cause-and-effect chain.

• Option 3 begins with "so she rented the latest romantic" without first establishing why she rented it, and places "she planned to try something different yesterday" illogically at the end.

• Option 4 begins with the consequence clause "so much so that", which cannot logically open the sentence since it has no preceding action to intensify.

NOTE

• Look for the segment that reads as a self-contained starting statement (no dangling connector like "so", "and", or "so much so that" at its head) — that segment must be placed first.

• "So much so that" is used to intensify a preceding statement, and therefore can never be the first segment in such a sequence.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
The police told the agitators to back in, else they would lathi-charge.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. the agitators to back in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrasal verb used — "back in" is not the correct phrase in this context.

• Rule: The correct phrasal verb to mean "to retreat or withdraw" (as agitators being asked to move away/retreat) is "back off" or "back away", not "back in".
◦ Correct: The police told the agitators to back off, else they would lathi-charge.

• The remaining parts of the sentence — "The police told", "else they would" (correct conditional connector), and "lathi-charge" (correctly used as a verb) — are all grammatically sound.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "lathi-charge" is correctly used here as a verb meaning to disperse a crowd by beating with batons — no error.

• Option 2: "else they would" is a correct conditional connector meaning "otherwise they would" — no error.

• Option 4: "The police told" is grammatically correct as the subject and reporting verb of the sentence — no error.

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs with "back": "back off" (to retreat/stop being aggressive), "back down" (to withdraw from a position or argument), "back up" (to support, or to move backward), "back out" (to withdraw from a commitment). "Back in" is not an established idiomatic phrase meaning retreat.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Data is being collected by the researcher.
option_3: The researcher has been collecting data.
option_4: The researcher will be collecting data.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The researcher is collecting data.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Data is being collected by the researcher" is in the Present Continuous Tense, Passive Voice (Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject).

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "the researcher" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "is" is retained (singular subject); the verb "being collected" becomes "is collecting"; and "Data" becomes the object.
◦ Active: The researcher is collecting data.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "has collected" is the active form of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Present Continuous Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "has been collecting" is the active form of the Present Perfect Continuous Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will be collecting" is the active form of the Future Continuous Tense.

NOTE

• Passive voice of continuous tenses always uses "being + V3"; do not confuse it with the passive of perfect tenses, which uses "been + V3" (without "being").

• Only the Simple Present, Simple Past, and continuous forms of Present/Past have a standard passive construction in SSC-level grammar; Future Continuous and Perfect Continuous passives are rarely used.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
His house is smaller than you .
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. is smaller than yours.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence wrongly compares "His house" (a thing) with "you" (a person) — this is a faulty/illogical comparison.

• Rule — Comparison of Possessives: When comparing a possession (e.g., "his house") with another person's equivalent possession, the possessive pronoun ("yours" = "your house") must be used, not the personal pronoun ("you"), so that like is compared with like.

• Applying the rule: "His house is smaller than yours" correctly compares "his house" with "your house" (yours).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "is small as you" is incorrect — the comparative degree requires "smaller than", not the positive degree "small as", and it still compares a house to a person.

• Option 3: "is small than you" is incorrect — the comparative adjective "smaller" must be used before "than", not the positive form "small".

• Option 4: "is smaller than your" is incorrect because "your" is a possessive adjective that must be followed by a noun (e.g., "your house") — it cannot stand alone as "yours" does.

NOTE

• Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) are used to avoid repeating a noun already mentioned and to keep comparisons logical.

• Common SSC error type: comparing a person's possession with another person directly (e.g., "My marks are better than him" — should be "better than his").

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
We took dinner in a Chinese restaurant and were amazed to see the interior of a restaurant.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. the interior of a restaurant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the use of the indefinite article "a" before "restaurant" in the second mention.

• Rule — Articles: The definite article "the" is used to refer to a noun that has already been mentioned or is specifically known to both speaker and listener, while "a/an" is used for a general, non-specific, first mention.

• Since the restaurant has already been specifically mentioned earlier in the sentence ("in a Chinese restaurant"), the second reference to the same restaurant must use "the", not "a".
◦ Correct: ...and were amazed to see the interior of the restaurant.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "and were amazed to see" is grammatically correct — a properly formed verb phrase joined with "and".

• Option 3: "We took dinner" is grammatically acceptable as the opening clause of the sentence — no error.

• Option 4: "in a Chinese restaurant" is correct — "a" is properly used here since the restaurant is being mentioned for the first time.

NOTE

• Article rule to remember: use "a/an" for the first, non-specific mention of a singular countable noun, and switch to "the" for every subsequent mention of that same, now-specific, noun.

• This is a very common SSC error-spotting pattern — watch for a noun repeated later in the sentence still carrying the indefinite article "a/an" instead of switching to "the".

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
Fundamentels of every subject need to be learnt on priority basis.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Fundamentels.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Fundamentals" — the basic principles or rules on which something is based.
◦ Example: Students must master the fundamentals of grammar before attempting advanced writing.

• Spelling key: the word ends in "-tals" (from "fundamental" + "s"), not "-tels". The incorrect form in the sentence wrongly substitutes an "e" for the "a" in the final syllable.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "priority" is correctly spelt — meaning the state of being treated as more important.

• Option 2: "basis" is correctly spelt — meaning the foundation or starting point for something.

• Option 4: "learnt" is correctly spelt — the British past tense/past participle form of "learn" (American English typically uses "learned").

NOTE

• Do not confuse the suffix "-al" (as in fundamental, essential, national) with "-el" — words ending in "-mental" are especially prone to this misspelling: e.g., environmental, departmental, monumental, incremental.

question: Out of the four sentences given, three have spelling errors. Identify the sentence that has no spelling error.
option_1: What advice did he give to young entreprenuers?
option_2: She tried to manoeuvre her trolley around people.
option_3: The computer's software detected an anamoly caused by a virus.
option_4: A clergyman read the litturgy from the prayer-book.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She tried to manoeuvre her trolley around people.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "manoeuvre" (a skilful movement or plan) is correctly spelt in Option 2. This is the British spelling; the American spelling is "maneuver".
◦ Example: The pilot had to manoeuvre the plane carefully to avoid the storm.

• Spelling key: M-A-N-O-E-U-V-R-E — note the unusual "oeu" sequence, a common source of SSC spelling traps.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "entreprenuers" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "entrepreneurs" (the "e" and "u" near the ending are wrongly interchanged).

• Option 3: "anamoly" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "anomaly" (meaning something that deviates from what is standard or expected); the "a" and "o" have been transposed.

• Option 4: "litturgy" is misspelt — the correct spelling is "liturgy" (meaning a form of public religious worship); it should have a single "t", not double.

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt SSC words in this family: entrepreneur, manoeuvre, anomaly, liturgy, bureaucracy, questionnaire, connoisseur — all borrowed from French/Greek/Latin with irregular English spellings worth memorising individually.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.
A person who is kept captive for fulfilment of demands of money or conditions
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Hostage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Hostage" is a person seized or held captive by another, in order to compel a third party to fulfil certain conditions, typically the payment of a ransom. (बंधक)
◦ Example: The kidnappers held the businessman hostage until the ransom was paid.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Hermit (सन्यासी) is a person who lives in solitude, especially for religious reasons — unrelated to being held captive.

• Option 3: Heretic (धर्मद्रोही) is a person holding beliefs that go against established religious doctrine — unrelated to captivity.

• Option 4: Introvert (अंतर्मुखी) is a shy, reticent person who prefers their own company — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes often tested by SSC: Captive (a person imprisoned or confined), Prisoner of war (a captured combatant held during war), Ransom (money demanded for the release of a hostage).

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

When Ojeya Cruz Banks moved to Ohio from New Zealand (1)_________ years ago, she was overwhelmed by the logistics of uprooting her life. But Cruz Banks, a Denison University professor and a single mom, who is also my neighbour and friend, was (2)_________ to find a house next to a public elementary school. She assumed that she would be able to walk to pick up her daughter, a needed convenience given that she didn’t yet have a car. Unfortunately, when she went to register her daughter for kindergarten, she was met with an (3)_________ surprise: The only (4)_________ option was a half-day program that would bus students to a day-care centre on the outskirts of the town for the afternoon. The district did offer a limited number of full-day slots, but those had all been claimed in a lottery earlier that spring and came with a tuition cost. “I was like, ‘Cost me? What? Public school costs money here?’” she told me.

Many parents across the United States, like Cruz Banks, may assume that free, full-day kindergarten is a (5)_________ part of the country’s public education system. I was one of them, until my youngest had to enter our district’s lottery several months ago. When he was assigned to the half-day program, I swung between alarm and frustration.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. several.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that can naturally precede "years ago" to indicate an unspecified but multiple number of years.

• "Several" means more than two but not very many; some, and is the standard word used with time expressions like "years ago", "months ago", "days ago".
◦ Example: He moved to this city several years ago.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "particular" means specific or distinct — it does not fit before "years ago", as no specific number or year has been indicated in the passage.

• Option 3: "enormous" means very large in size or extent — it is used for size/magnitude, not typically for a span of years in this idiomatic sense; "enormous years" is not natural usage.

• Option 4: "immense" similarly means extremely large — like "enormous", it does not collocate naturally with "years ago".

NOTE

• Common collocations with time spans: "several years ago", "a few years ago", "many years ago" — words like "enormous" and "immense" collocate with size/quantity/degree (e.g., "immense pressure", "enormous crowd"), not with spans of time.

• In cloze passages, always check what word naturally "collocates" (habitually goes together) with the surrounding words, not just what fits the general meaning.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. relieved.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes Cruz Banks finding a house next to a public elementary school as a positive development — it gave her the convenience of being able to walk to pick up her daughter, since she did not have a car.

• "Relieved" means feeling reassured and free from anxiety or distress, typically after an outcome favourable to oneself. This fits the positive, fortunate tone of finding a conveniently located house.
◦ Example: She felt relieved to finally find affordable housing close to work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "distraught" means deeply upset or agitated — this would suggest a negative reaction, which contradicts the passage's context of the house being a needed convenience.

• Option 2: "dispassionate" means not influenced by strong emotion; impartial — this does not fit, as the context calls for an emotional (positive) reaction, not neutrality.

• Option 4: "worried" means anxious or troubled — this contradicts the favourable outcome described (finding a conveniently located house).

NOTE

• Cloze passages often test whether the tone of the surrounding sentence (positive/negative) matches the connotation of the chosen word — here the clue is "a needed convenience", which signals a positive/relieved emotion, not a negative one.

• Words of relief and reassurance often tested by SSC: relieved, reassured, comforted, at ease.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. unpleasant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence following the blank explains what the "surprise" actually was: the only option available was a half-day program that bused children to a distant day-care centre, while full-day slots required a lottery and a tuition cost — clearly an undesirable, disappointing situation for Cruz Banks.

• "Unpleasant" means causing discomfort or displeasure; disagreeable, which correctly matches this negative outcome.
◦ Example: He got an unpleasant surprise when he saw the size of the repair bill.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "agreeable" means pleasing or pleasant — this contradicts the negative situation described immediately after the blank.

• Option 3: "amusing" means causing laughter or providing entertainment — inappropriate for a serious, frustrating situation about school registration.

• Option 4: "enjoyable" means giving pleasure or satisfaction — again the opposite of the disappointing situation described in the passage.

NOTE

• When filling a blank followed by a colon or explanation, always read ahead — the explanation that follows the blank (here, the inconvenient half-day program) usually confirms whether the missing word should be positive or negative.

• Synonyms of "unpleasant" often tested by SSC: disagreeable, unwelcome, distasteful, unfavourable.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. available.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that only one option — the half-day program — existed for Cruz Banks' daughter, since the full-day slots had already been claimed through a lottery. This means the half-day program was the only option that could actually be accessed/obtained.

• "Available" means able to be used or obtained; at one's disposal, which correctly describes the single option that was actually open to her.
◦ Example: The only available seats on the train were in the last coach.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "futile" means incapable of producing any useful result; pointless — this would not describe an "option" that a parent could still choose and use.

• Option 3: "nonviable" means not able to work successfully; not feasible — this contradicts the fact that she actually used the half-day program (it clearly was feasible, if not ideal).

• Option 4: "inaccessible" means unable to be reached or obtained — this is self-contradictory, since the passage states this option was in fact taken up.

NOTE

• "Available" is the standard word to describe an option that exists and can be chosen/accessed, as opposed to words like "inaccessible" or "nonviable" which describe options that cannot be used at all.

• Do not let a negative-sounding surrounding context (the situation being disappointing) mislead you into choosing a negative-sounding word for every blank — judge each blank on its own required meaning within its immediate clause.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. required.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage explains that many parents assume free, full-day kindergarten is a standard, guaranteed part of the public education system — an assumption the writer says was mistaken, since her own child ended up in a half-day program via a lottery.

• "Required" means needed or necessary; a mandatory/expected part of something, which fits the sense that people expect full-day kindergarten to be a standard, guaranteed element of public education.
◦ Example: Attending morning assembly is a required part of the school routine.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "disapproved" means having an unfavourable opinion of something — this makes no logical sense as a description of a "part" of the education system.

• Option 2: "ceaseless" means without pause or interruption — this does not describe an expected/standard component of a system; it describes something continuous or unending.

• Option 3: "inessential" means not absolutely necessary — this directly contradicts the passage's point, since parents assumed full-day kindergarten WAS a necessary, guaranteed part of public education (the opposite of inessential).

NOTE

• The passage's central theme is the mistaken assumption that full-day kindergarten is guaranteed/necessary — so the blank must carry a sense of necessity or standard inclusion, matching "required".

• Synonyms of "required" often tested by SSC: essential, mandatory, necessary, obligatory, compulsory.
